header.author: Isidorus Hispalensis
header.source: Translated by Claude (claude-opus-5-5, Anthropic) from the library's tmp1430.tmp1430.opp-lat1, from Open Greek and Latin's Patrologia Latina (CC BY-SA 4.0), one English line for each line of the original. notes.urn:cts:latinLit:tmp1430.tmp1430.opp-lat: 2.6: 'patriarchaeum' read as 'patriarcharum'; 'qui ex passionibus lanii' is evidently corrupt, read as 'homo' (man), matching the God/man contrast. 2.9: 'per illusionem sancti Spiritus' is probably a misprint for 'infusionem' (or 'illustrationem'); translated as 'infusion'. 2.8: 'appropinquabit' (future) kept as printed, though the usual text has 'appropinquavit'.

3.2: 'moi' read as 'mox' (at once). 4.3: 'vitia coccinea' read as 'vitta coccinea' (scarlet ribbon), as in the Vulgate; 'agate' read as 'agat'. 4.4: 'latetur' read as 'fatetur' (confesses). 4.6: 'in passinis' read as 'in passionis'.

4.9: 'austeritate regis' read as 'legis' (law), as the context requires. 4.10: 'it littera' read as 'in littera'. 5.4: 'cum colo' is evidently corrupt; rendered 'I rest' (perhaps 'conquiesco'). 5.5: 'frigens claritas' read as 'frigens charitas' (cooling charity). 5.6: 'reveLant' read as 'repetam'; 'se retæ' read as 'semel'. 5.11: 'tulamen' read as 'velamen' (veil).

6.5: the explanation of the numbers seems defective; as printed it applies 'the perfection of the number six, through ten' to the concubines, though it surely belongs to the sixty queens (an explanation of eighty seems lost). 6.9: 'Noli tui bata e?se' is corrupt; read tentatively as 'noli tibi data esse' ('do not be given over to yourself'). 7.1: the printed text breaks off with dots. Scanning errors silently corrected throughout (e.g. lucte/lacte, contemplum/contemptum, lacUs/factis, firluitatis/firmitatis, proliciunt/proficiunt, die/dic).

7.2: 'spirituali prope fecundorum' read as 'spirituali prole fecundorum' (fruitful with spiritual offspring). 7.7: 'alligamur' read as 'alligantur'. 7.12: 'callem ad propositum ... assurgere' is odd; possibly corrupt (perhaps for 'mane', echoing 'mane surgamus'); rendered literally as 'rise to the path'. 7.13: the lemma has 'in hortis' (gardens) but the comment speaks of 'portæ'/'portis' (gates), perhaps a variant reading 'in portis nostris'; translated as printed. 8.3: 'lætis ducam in dolium matris meæ luminibus' read as 'in domum', 'with joyful eyes'.

8.10: 'quasi 'urnis' read as 'quasi turris'; 'omuia maligni expellere' read as 'omnia maligni' (all [the attacks] of the wicked one), possibly 'omnia maligna'. 8.12: 'argentes' read as 'argenteos'. 8.13: 'I ortis' and 'buflis' read as 'hortis'. 8.14: 'omni dilecte' is probably a misreading of 'o mi dilecte'.

nodes.text: APPENDIX VI.
EXPOSITION OF THE SONG OF SONGS OF SOLOMON.

CHAPTER I. — 1. Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth. Let him touch me with the sweetness of his presence, he whom I have often heard promised by the prophets. For your breasts are better than wine. The sweetness of the gospel teaching is better than the severity of the law. Fragrant with the best ointments. With the gifts of the Holy Spirit: from chrism [comes] Christ, that is, anointed from anointing, a name that is poured out on all the faithful in baptism together with the grace of the Holy Spirit. Therefore the maidens have loved you. The souls of the elect, renewed by the grace of baptism.

2. Draw me after you. So that I may follow you as you ascend into heaven. The king has brought me into his storerooms. By faith, into the inner joys of the heavenly homeland. We will exult and rejoice in you, mindful of your breasts above wine. In you, not in ourselves; mindful in all things that the grace of faith is above the teaching of the law. The upright love you. No one loves you unless he is upright; and no one is upright unless he loves you. I am black but beautiful, daughters of Jerusalem. The voice of the Church about her afflictions. Black in the afflictions of persecutions, but beautiful in the comeliness of virtues.

3. Like the tents of Kedar, like the skins of Solomon. Darkened in the temptation of demons, beautiful in putting to death fleshly desires. Do not look at me because I am dark, for the sun has discoloured me. Do not wonder if I am despised outwardly by men because of the heat of temptations. The sons of my mother fought against me; they made me keeper in the vineyards; my own vineyard I did not keep. The bitterness of the sons of the Synagogue made me not keep the vineyard at Jerusalem, but become keeper of many vineyards, that is, of the Churches throughout the world. Show me, you whom my soul loves, where you pasture, where you lie at noon, lest I begin to wander after the flocks of your companions. Show me my shepherd, whom I love with my whole mind, and among whom he has pasture and rest, lest, troubled by the heat of temptations, I begin to seek him through the conventicles of companions, that is, of heretics.

4. If you do not know yourself, O fairest among women, go out, and go away after the tracks of your flocks. If you do not know that you are betrothed to me under such a condition of temptations, go out from my sight, and follow the various doings of those who stray. And pasture your kids beside the tents of the shepherds. That is, nourish lost hearers, having followed the teachings of foolish masters. To my cavalry among Pharaoh's chariots I have likened you, my friend. As I freed the former people from fear of the Egyptian, so I will free you, my bride, from empty threats, if you trust in me.

5. Your cheeks are beautiful, like a turtledove's. I have adorned you with such virtue of saving modesty that you will corrupt the chastity of the faith pledged to me by no seduction of wicked teachers. Your neck is like necklaces; we will make you golden chains inlaid with silver. By the neck teachers are signified. By the necklaces works are expressed, because what they teach in word they show in works. By the chains Sacred Scripture is shown, which shines inwardly with the gold of spiritual senses, and gleams outwardly with the silver of heavenly speech.

6. While the king was on his couch, my nard gave forth its fragrance. That is, while Christ rests in the blessedness of the heavenly secret place, the virtue of the saints ministers to us the grace of great sweetness. A bundle of myrrh is my beloved to me; he will dwell between my breasts. The death of my beloved, which he underwent for my salvation, will always dwell in my memory. A cluster of cypress is my beloved to me in the vineyards of En-gedi. He who was a bundle of myrrh in the bitterness of the passion is himself a cluster of cypress in the sweetness of the resurrection. Myrrh saddens, wine gladdens. In the vineyards of En-gedi, because of the divine gifts which after the resurrection he bestowed in baptism on those who share in him. En-gedi, 'spring of the kid', signifies baptism.

7. Behold, you are beautiful, my friend, behold, you are beautiful. Beautiful in simplicity of heart and purity of works. Your eyes are doves'. Because your senses are endowed with spiritual understanding.

8. Behold, you are beautiful, my beloved, behold, you are beautiful. You alone are beautiful by nature; I am beautiful from you. Our bed is flowering. The peace of holy Church both flowers with holy virtues and is multiplied with spiritual offspring. The beams of our houses are of cedar; our panelled ceilings of cypress. The beams and ceilings are the teachers in holy Church, because of protection and adornment. Of cedar and cypress because of their outstanding virtues and the fragrance of a good life.

CHAPTER II. — 1. I am the flower of the field, and the lily of the valleys. I am the glory of the world, and the glory of the humble. As a lily among thorns, so is my friend among the daughters. You seek rest and the praises of the bed; remember that you are made whiter by the thorns of tribulations, and that the fruit of preaching is greater than that of quiet.

2. As the apple tree among the trees of the woods, so is my beloved among the sons. As the apple tree surpasses the forest trees in look, smell and taste, so Christ surpasses all the saints, who are called sons of God, but by grace, he alone by nature. I sat under the shade of him whom I had desired. Under the protection of him whom I always sought to have near, I rest and remain secure. And his fruit is sweet to my throat. Because he has refreshed me with the sweetness of his heavenly grace.

3. He brought me into the wine cellar; he set charity in order in me. The wine cellar must be understood as the Church, in whose unity alone the Holy Spirit is customarily given and received, whose grace is signified in this place by the name of wine. In this cellar charity is set in order, so that one loves God with the whole heart more than oneself. Prop me up with flowers, surround me with apples, for I languish with love. Console me with the examples of those either beginning or completing the way of salvation, while I still languish, in the weariness of this pilgrimage, with love of the heavenly vision. His left hand is under my head, and his right hand will embrace me. By Christ's left hand his temporal goods are signified, by the right the blessedness of eternal life. For here he strengthens the mind through hope, and there he glorifies it through reward.

4. I adjure you, daughters of Jerusalem, by the roes and the harts of the fields, that you do not stir up nor make the beloved awake until she herself wishes. I solemnly charge the peaceable souls of the faithful, each by her own virtues, which are signified by the clean and ruminating animals, not to hinder the devout pursuits of their brothers by any importunity; but let each rejoice in his neighbour's progress as in his own.

5. The voice of my beloved. Understood: this is; whom I heard adjuring the daughters of Jerusalem not to stir me up as I rest in his embrace. Behold, he comes leaping on the mountains, bounding over the hills. For my beloved made such leaps: from heaven he came into the womb, from the womb into the manger, from the manger onto the cross, from the cross into the tomb, from the tomb he returned into heaven. He it is who is raised above all mountains and hills, that is, the heights of the saints.

6. My beloved is like a roe, and a young hart. In the assumption of flesh and in humility Christ is compared to the roe; in the variety of virtues and in innocence to the young of the harts, that is, of the patriarchs. See, he stands behind our wall, looking through the windows, gazing through the lattices. Clothed with the wall of our mortality he lay hidden, but looking out towards us through the lattices and windows he worked miracles, so that from the miracles he might appear God, who from his sufferings [appeared] man. See, my beloved speaks to me. He urges me to preach, saying:

7. Arise, make haste, my friend, my beautiful one, and come. Arise from the couch of quiet, on which you seek to take care of yourself alone; make haste and come, to bestow the care of salvation on your neighbours too, through the zeal of diligent preaching. For now the winter is past, the rain is over and gone. Now the cold of unbelief and the rain of iniquity have departed, which covered the whole world up to the time of the Lord's incarnation. The flowers have appeared in our land. That is, the beginnings of faith and justice have flowered in the world as the Church grows.

8. The time of pruning has come. That is, so that, the useless shoots of vain religion being cut away, the hearts of men may be prepared for the future fruit of faith. The voice of the turtledove has been heard in our land. That is, [the voice] of Christ our Saviour saying: Do penance, for the kingdom of heaven will draw near. The fig tree has put forth its green figs. The precepts of the old law have fallen. The flowering vines have given their fragrance. That is, the gospel people, or the vines flowering with holy conduct, have given fragrance far and wide.

9. Arise, make haste, my friend, my lovely one, and come; my dove, in the clefts of the rock, in the hollow of the wall. O bride and friend, to whom I have offered such great goods, arise and come; gird yourself for the contest, from which you will receive eternal rest. My dove, through the infusion of the Holy Spirit. In the clefts of the rock, that is, in the wounds which the bridegroom received for the salvation of the bride. In the hollow of the wall, that is, in the guard of the heavenly powers. Show me your face, let your voice sound in my ears. The voice, namely, of praise or of preaching. For your voice is sweet and your face comely. For his voice is sweet to the Lord to whom it is sweet either to proclaim the word of the Lord or to sound forth praises to the Lord himself. And that faith is comely which, adorned with works, does not fear to suffer adversity.

10. Catch us the little foxes that destroy the vineyards. That is, overcome the heretics and schismatics, perverse in faith and deceitful in word, who are accustomed to tear the untaught minds of the faithful with the tooth of perverse doctrine. For our vineyard has flowered. That is, the peoples of the elect are sprouting far and wide.

11. My beloved is mine, and I am his. That is, he alone is my beloved, and he alone is my helper. And I alone am beloved by him, because no other rightly loves Christ except the one Church, and no other is loved by him. Who feeds among the lilies. That is, in the purity of faith and the whiteness of the virtues. Until the day breathes and the shadows decline. Until the eternal light of the age to come rises, and the shadows, that is, the errors of the present life, pass away. Return, be like a roe, and a young hart upon the mountains of Bether. I beseech [you], my beloved, to return to me more often with the sweetness of your visitation, you who in the flesh, which you took from the stock of the patriarchs, ascended above all the heights of the heavenly mountains, so that you may relieve the toil of my pilgrimage with the contemplation of the eternal homeland.

CHAP. III. — 1. On my little bed by night I sought him whom my soul loves; I sought, and did not find [him]. For a long time now, she says, I have sought the Lord with great zeal; but because I was still subject to the allurements of my flesh and blinded by the darkness of ignorance, I did not find the light of truth, that is, the Lord. I will rise and go about the city; in the streets and squares I will seek him whom my soul loves; I sought him and did not find [him]. I resolved in my mind to rise from the little bed of carnal pleasures, to go about lands and seas, and to hear the teachings of the philosophers; but not even so did I find him.

2. The watchmen who guard the city found me. Have you seen him whom my soul loves? The watchmen who guard the Church are the apostles and teachers, who found the Gentile world by their anxious search for the truth. When I had passed them by a little, I found him whom my soul loves. As soon as I gave myself over to their teaching, I at once found the light of truth which I had sought. I held him, and I will not let [him] go until I bring him into my mother's house and into the chamber of her who bore me. I hold him with firm faith, until at the end of the age, through the office of preaching, I bring him into the house and into the chamber of the Synagogue, which bore me in the Lord, and there may be one fold and one shepherd.

3. I adjure you, daughters of Jerusalem, etc. The bridegroom repeats this verse so that he may not be thought to have less care for the Church gathered from the Gentiles than for [that] from the Jews, but so that from both there may be one bride, and she most beloved.

4. Who is this who comes up through the desert? The Synagogue wonders how the people of the Gentiles, amended by no mystery of circumcision, instructed by no admonition of the prophets, had suddenly come up from the lowest pleasures, through the desert of idolatry and paganism, to the lofty summits of the virtues and the embraces of the bridegroom. Like a column of smoke from spices. Kindled by the fire of love, she strives with every effort of the virtues toward heavenly things.

5. Of myrrh and frankincense, and of every powder of the perfumer. From the mortification of carnal pleasures, and the purity of prayers, and the fragrance of all the virtues. Behold, sixty mighty men of the mightiest of Israel surround the little bed of Solomon. The little bed of Solomon is the way of life of the saints; the sixty mighty men are the holy preachers and most valiant warriors, who, pure in heart, are worthy to see the Lord.

6. All holding swords, and most skilled in war. For they hold the sword of the spirit, which is the word of God, who fulfil in deed what they teach with the mouth. Each one's sword upon his thigh because of fears in the night. Fears in the night are in the day of hidden temptation. The preacher's sword is watchful guard, repressing the lusts of the flesh, so that impurity of life may not stain the word of preaching.

7. King Solomon made himself a litter of the wood of Lebanon. The litter of Solomon is the holy Church, which lifts believers to the banquet of eternal blessedness, and which is built from those strong in spirit as from wood that does not rot. He made its pillars of silver, the back of gold. The silver pillars are the teachers, shining with the light of eloquence. The golden back is the perpetual hope of rest promised to the faithful.

8. The ascent of purple. What is the purple ascent, if not the blood of the martyrs and the passion of our Redeemer? For one does not ascend to the banquet of life except through the mystery of Christ's passion. The middle he covered with charity for the daughters of Jerusalem. For everyone who has charity toward God and neighbour will come joyfully to this rest and to this banquet. Christ bestowed all these ornaments on the Church because of the exceeding charity with which he loved us and gave himself up for us.

9. Go forth and see, daughters of Zion, King Solomon. Go forth in mind and in action from the way of life of the turbulent world, so that you may be able to see the king of peace. In the diadem with which his mother crowned him. See the Lord Christ in the humanity which, taken from the Virgin mother, he set at the right hand of the Father's majesty. On the day of his espousal. That is, at the time of his incarnation, when he came forth from the virginal womb to join the Church to himself as bride. On the day of the gladness of his heart. That is, [the day] of the redemption of the human race, which was the day of Christ's gladness.

CHAP. IV. — 1. How beautiful you are, my friend, how beautiful you are! He calls the Church beautiful, and repeats 'beautiful', because he saw that she was praiseworthy both in action and in preaching. Your eyes are [those] of doves. Your senses are excellent and venerable in the contemplation of spiritual things. Besides that which lies hidden within. Great indeed is the glory of open work, but far more incomparable [is that] of the eternal reward, which cannot yet be seen.

2. Your hair is like flocks of goats. In the hair may be understood the faithful peoples, who by their number give the greatest beauty to the Church. Which have come up from Mount Gilead. Gilead is interpreted 'heap of testimony', which fits well the gathered multitude of the saints. Your teeth are like flocks of shorn [ewes]. In the hair the weaker, but in the teeth the more perfect, those fit to rule the Church, are signified.

3. Which have come up from the washing. That is, from the font of holy baptism, who are as it were shorn and washed, that is, stripped by renouncing the world and cleansed by the washing of life. All with twin offspring, and there is none barren among them. There is none among them who does not bring forth the offspring of good work. Your lips are like a scarlet ribbon, and your speech is sweet. The scarlet ribbon is understood as the teaching of truth. The bride's lips are likened to scarlet because the Church does not cease to preach the price of the Lord's blood by which she was redeemed, or because holy preaching blazes with the ardour of charity.

4. Like the rind of a pomegranate are your cheeks. In the cheeks modesty is expressed, in the pomegranate the passion of Christ. So the bride has the redness of the pomegranate in her cheeks when she confesses the sacrament of the Lord's cross in words and proves it in deeds. Like the tower of David is your neck. The tower is the Church, the neck the preachers, whose faith and constancy is firm in that same city and impregnable on every side. Which is built with bulwarks. The bulwarks of this city are the defences of the holy Scriptures, or of the outstanding Fathers.

5. A thousand shields hang from it. For as many precepts as there are in the divine books, so many are the defences of our breast, by which we are protected against all snares. All the armour of the mighty. All the equipment, whether of heavenly practice or of heavenly teaching, by which we not only escape but also overcome. Your two breasts are like two twin fawns of a roe, which feed among the lilies, until the day breathes and the shadows decline. The two breasts are the two peoples coming from the circumcision and from the Gentiles; who through humility indeed understand themselves to be little and sinners, but, running in charity, pass over all the obstacles of the world; who feed among the lilies, that is, on the most radiant examples of the holy Fathers, until, as the eternal day breathes, we pass beyond the shadows of the present mortality.

6. I will go to the mountain of myrrh and to the hill of frankincense. In myrrh the mortification of the flesh is expressed, in frankincense the devotion of prayer; as if the bridegroom were saying: I will visit often, and graciously glorify with holy illumination, those whom I perceive to be lofty in the virtue of suffering or of prayer.

7. Come from Lebanon, my bride, come from Lebanon. Lebanon is interpreted 'whiteness', that is, the soul made white by good deeds, whom the bridegroom urges three times to come: first, living in the flesh, through good works; second, released from the flesh, to receive the blessed life; third, having received back the body, to enjoy the perfect joys after the resurrection.

8. You will be crowned from the head of Amana, from the summit of Senir and Hermon, from the dens of lions, from the mountains of leopards. The lions, for their pride, and the leopards, for their cruelty, are the evil spirits; the mountains of Amana signify the proud hearts of unbelievers, where the unclean spirits have their seat. When the holy preachers convert such men to the way of salvation, they are crowned from the head and summit of the mountains, that is, from the chiefs of the proud, because the crown of glory grows from the toil of the contest.

9. You have wounded my heart, my sister, my bride, you have wounded my heart. In the wounding of the heart the greatness of Christ's love in the Church is understood. With one of your eyes, and with one hair of your neck. That is, in the holy unity of the teachers, that is, of the eyes, and in the holy unity of the people, that is, of the hairs. How beautiful are your breasts, my sister, my bride. Likewise, by the name of breasts the holy teachers are signified, because of the comfort of the weak and the nourishing of the little ones, which is expressed by milk. Your breasts are more beautiful than wine. The sweetness of grace is more beautiful than the severity of the law. And the fragrance of your ointments is above all spices. The most sweet fame of the faith, spread through the whole world, is wider than that of the old law and of the fathers in it, which was confined to Judaea alone.

10. Your lips, bride, are a dripping honeycomb. A honeycomb is honey in wax. Now honey in wax is the spiritual sense of divine things in the letter; [the honeycomb is] dripping honey, because almost every single sentence has manifold senses. The lips are the spirit of the teachers, who reveal that manifold senses are present in the sacred writings. Honey and milk are under your tongue. In milk the instruction of the little ones is signified, in honey the more perfect teaching of the stronger; under the tongue, that is, in the meditation of the heart.

11. And the fragrance of your garments is like the fragrance of frankincense. The garments of the Church are her works, which are compared to the fragrance of frankincense, because all the holy things that the Church does for the Lord take the place of prayers on her behalf. A garden enclosed, my sister, my bride, a garden enclosed, a fountain sealed. The Church is a garden, because she brings forth manifold shoots of spiritual works; she is a fountain, because she overflows with saving teaching; enclosed, because she remains fortified by the Lord's protection; sealed, by the word of faith.

12. Your outflowings are a paradise of pomegranates, with the fruits of the orchard. Through the watering of holy baptism the holy Church has sent forth from herself a paradise of pomegranates, that is, of the holy martyrs; with the fruits of the orchard, that is, with the fruit of holy virtues. Cypress with nard, nard and saffron. The cypress is an aromatic tree, and it signifies the blessing of heavenly grace. Nard expresses a figure of the Lord's passion; saffron, the fervour of charity. Cypress is joined to nard when divine grace strengthens us to suffer for Christ; likewise nard is joined to saffron when, out of love for Christ, we willingly undergo death.

13. Cane and cinnamon, with all the trees of Lebanon. Cane, which is also [called] cassia, is an aromatic tree, but a small one, and so it signifies the humble in spirit. Likewise cinnamon signifies those who think little of themselves. It too is a short tree, but fragrant and sweet; for humility has great praise and sweetness with the Lord. With all the trees of Lebanon. Just as cane and cinnamon signify the humble thoughts of the saints, the trees of Lebanon show their lofty deeds. Myrrh and aloes are aromatic trees, which express the continence of the flesh.

14. With all the chief ointments. That is, with the more excellent gifts of the virtues; and the joining of these trees is fitting, because when we restrain the flesh from wantonness, it follows that we receive greater gifts of the Spirit. A fountain of gardens, a well of living waters, which flow with force from Lebanon. Both are the Church: she is a fountain of gardens, because she brings forth spiritual fruits, and a well of living waters which flow with force from Lebanon, because of the hidden mysteries which are opened to the saints alone through the revelation of the Holy Spirit; of living waters, because of the divine utterances, which proceed from the invisible treasuries of divine grace; from Lebanon: he speaks of the Church herself, who is both white through the purity of faith and lofty through the virtue of glory.

15. Arise, north wind, and come, south wind, blow through my garden. For in the north wind the adversities of the world are signified, in the south wind its allurements, by which twofold assault the Church is tested. 'Arise' is the voice of one permitting, not of one commanding. And let its spices flow. That is, let it spread abroad the constancy of the virtues with a wonderful fragrance.

CHAP. V. — 1. Let my beloved come into his garden. Let the Lord come into his Church, so that he himself may keep her spotless everywhere, and make her fruitful with the harvest of faith. And let him eat the fruit of his orchard. And let him willingly receive and gladly look upon the works of his servants.

2. I have come into my garden, my sister, my bride. I have come, he says, very often into my Church, and I come, to correct, help and strengthen [her]. I have reaped my myrrh with my spices. By myrrh suffering or mortification is expressed, by spices all the virtues. He reaps myrrh with spices when he brings the martyrs, with the other elect, to the ripeness of their rewards.

3. I have eaten the honeycomb with my honey, I have drunk the wine with my milk. In the honeycomb and the wine the preachers are understood, in the honey and the milk the hearers, and the inner judge approves and rewards both. Eat, friends, and drink, and be drunk, dearest ones. Friends, by doing what I command, I beg you, so fill your hearts with the deeds of the saints, as with choice feasts.

4. I sleep. By the gift of God's grace, I rest in the peace of the present life. And my heart keeps watch. The more calmly I rest amid outward assaults, the more deeply I see within how good God is. The voice of my beloved knocking. He knocks at the door of the heart when the Lord rouses us to progress in the virtues. Open to me, that is, open your heart to me, my sister. My friend, because you share my secrets. My dove, because you are illumined by the gift of my Spirit. My spotless one, because you alone are worthy of my sight.

5. For my head is full of dew, and my locks of the drops of the nights. The head of Christ is God. The locks are the gatherings of the faithful. In the dew and the drops of the nights is shown the cooling charity in many, which they ought to have had toward the Lord and their neighbours. Therefore the Lord of necessity rouses all the faithful to zeal for preaching, and the Church, so called to the labour of teaching, answers.

6. I have taken off my tunic; how shall I put it on? As if she were saying openly: I have left worldly business for your sake; how shall I take it up again? I have washed my feet; how shall I defile them? I have once washed away earthly thoughts with tears of compunction; how shall I be polluted again with the filth of the world? For the office of preaching can hardly exist without worldly occupation.

7. My beloved put his hand through the opening. The beloved indeed put his hand through the opening when the Lord, by hidden compunction, invisibly kindles us to the work of the virtues, and calls back to our memory how and how much he suffered for us, coming down from the bosom of the Father. And my belly trembled at his touch. The bride, recalling these things in her inmost conscience, is wholly struck with fear; and, accusing the sloth of her rest, she hastens to the labour of preaching; whence follows:

8. I arose to open to my beloved. That is, to preach the word of the Lord. My hands dripped myrrh, and my fingers were full of the choicest myrrh. For in the hands works are signified, in the fingers discernment; in myrrh continence and sufferings, which are most choice when continence is practised, or sufferings borne, solely for the love of God and neighbour.

9. I opened the bolt of my door to my beloved. He opens the bolt to the beloved who has made the temple of his breast worthy of the divine visiting and indwelling. He had turned aside and gone by. Because to no one in this life is the full vision of God granted, as it is in the life to come, the beloved is therefore said to go by, that is, he shows that he is to be seen and enjoyed more fully in the future.

10. My soul melted when my beloved spoke. The more sweetly, she says, I received the voice and nearness of my beloved, the more deeply whatever in me was cold grew warm with charity, and whatever was stiff melted. I sought, and did not find him. Because the gift of compunction and of inner sweetness lies not in the choice of the one who wills, but in the mercy of the one who gives, [the faithful] therefore do not always have him equally, because God does not offer himself to those toiling in exile as he does to those reigning in the homeland.

11. The watchmen who go about the city found me, they struck me, they wounded me; the keepers of the walls took my cloak from me. The keepers of the city, that is, of the Church, are the holy teachers, who with diligent preaching go about the hearts of each person, and wound them with the darts of heavenly love, and inflame them so that they may burn the more, and draw away from them the veil of their old way of life.

12. I adjure you, daughters of Jerusalem, if you find my beloved, that you tell him that I languish with love. Rightly does the bride languish, since, struck by the sword of God's word, she puts off her earthly garment; and she adjures the daughters of Jerusalem, that is, souls worthy of God, to report the greatness of her love to the Lord, and to ask heavenly help for her that she may see his glory.

13. What is your beloved beyond [any other] beloved, O most beautiful of women? What is your beloved beyond [any other] beloved, that you have so adjured us? I beg you, since you have so adjured me, that by the word of preaching you make me too burn with the love with which you say you languish, and show me what your beloved is like in that respect in which he can be loved, not feared, because perfect charity casts out fear.

14. My beloved is white and ruddy, chosen out of thousands. White, because without sin; ruddy with the blood of the passion: Christ, who alone is the mediator of God and men. His head is the finest gold. The head of Christ is God, who alone is good and best. His locks are like the spathes of palms, black as a raven. The locks are the companies of the saints, who cling to God in faithful service. They are spathes, or choice palms, because of Christ the head; black because of afflictions.

15. His eyes are like doves beside the streams of waters. His eyes are the teachers, through whom the Church sees what is right; they are well compared to doves for their simplicity, and to streams of waters for the divine gifts of grace. Which are washed with milk, and sit beside the fullest flowings. It calls them washed with milk, that is, cleansed by divine and most sweet grace; and they sit beside the fullest flowings, that is, the abundance of all spiritual gifts. By the streams the learning of the old law can be signified, and by the fullest flowings the perfection of the gospel teaching, because holy preachers bring forth from their treasures things new and old.

16. His cheeks are like beds of spices planted by the perfumers; his lips are lilies dripping the first myrrh. In the cheeks of our Saviour both gentle mercy and at the same time severity are expressed. By the beds of spices virtues, sweetness and good report are signified. Planted by the perfumers, the prophets and apostles, the former telling the mysteries of his future incarnation, the latter its accomplishment. His lips are the words of his teaching. Lilies, because they promise the brightness of the heavenly kingdom. Dripping the first myrrh, because they preach that this is to be reached through contempt of present pleasures.

17. His hands are turned [on the lathe], golden, full of hyacinths. The hands, that is, the works, because what he taught in words he fulfilled in deeds. Turned, because they hold in themselves every rule of justice. Hence he says: It behoves me to fulfil all justice. And the hands are golden, because all that he did in [his] manhood he accomplished with the riches of glory. Full of hyacinths, because they rouse us to the hope and love of heavenly things, since the hyacinth is a gem of golden colour.

18. His belly is of ivory, set with sapphires. The belly of the beloved signifies the frailty of his humanity, ivory the beauty of chastity. The sapphire is the loftiness of the heavenly virtues. Set with sapphires, because in part human frailty is perceived, in hunger, temptation, weariness and death, and in part divine loftiness, in miracles, the resurrection and the ascension of glory.

19. His legs are pillars of marble, which are founded upon bases of gold. By the word legs the journeys of Christ's incarnation are suggested, which are compared to marble pillars for their firmness and straightness. Founded upon bases of gold, because whatever was done concerning him or through him was all ordered by the counsel of divine providence before the ages of the world.

20. His appearance is like Lebanon, chosen like the cedars. As Lebanon surpasses other mountains in height and in the beauty of its trees, so the Lord Christ surpasses all the saints in the height of his merits and the beauty of his virtues. Chosen like the cedars. As the cedars surpass in their dignity the other trees that grow on Lebanon, so Christ by his glory transcends all who are born to life in the Church.

21. His throat is most sweet. In the throat is recalled the inward sweetness of his words, which whoever tastes does not hunger. And he is wholly desirable. What more do you seek? He is wholly desirable, because he is wholly God and wholly man, into whom even the angels desire to look. God in the majesty of the Father, man in the virginity of the mother. In the one creator, in the other saviour.

22. Such is my beloved, and he is my friend. The more devoutly anyone loves the Lord, the more intimately he has the Lord as friend. And you must understand him to be such, if you wish to have him as friend. Where has your beloved gone, O most beautiful of women? The voice of the Synagogue; for to adorn the song the persons speaking together are varied. But only the Church of Christ, since it is expressed by the word bride, is designated most beautiful of women. The individual churches of the saints are beautiful; but most beautiful is the whole body of the entire holy Church throughout the whole world. Where has your beloved turned aside, and we will seek him with you? He who once dwelt on earth in bodily form, tell [us] where he has turned aside, that we may follow him with you.

CHAP. VI. — 1. My beloved has gone down into his garden, to the bed of spices. As if she had said, he went down there into the garden, that is, his Church, to water it with the fountain of his glory, like a bed of spices, so that it might sprout with the flowers of the virtues. To feed in the gardens and gather lilies. I prepare in myself a place of dwelling for my beloved, and he [prepares one] for me with himself, who is always fed among the holy desires of chaste minds. Up to here it is the voice of the holy Church seeking and praising; now what the one sought answers is added.

2. You are beautiful, my friend, sweet and comely as Jerusalem. He calls his holy Church friend, because the desire of her life is already likened to the vision of inmost peace. Terrible as an army of camps set in array. That is, united and knit together by charity, so that no place is opened to the enemy through the evil of discord, because only in the unity of peace are we terrible to the enemy.

3. Turn your eyes away from me, for they have made me fly away. That is, do not seek with the eyes of your mind to know me perfectly on the road of your pilgrimage, because that cannot be; for the more intently you seek to know [me], the more surely you will understand [me to be] incomprehensible; and do not seek on the way the reward that is kept in the homeland. Your hair is like flocks of goats, etc. These verses were set down earlier, but repetition is a sign of firmness. In the hair the peoples are understood, in the teeth the teachers, in the twin offspring the precepts of charity.

4. Like the rind of a pomegranate, so are your cheeks, besides what is hidden within you. The cheeks of the holy Church are the spiritual Fathers, who are wonderful in virtues and venerable in conduct, and not ashamed to glory in the cross of Christ. And very great are these things that are seen in her; but much greater are those that are not seen and are kept for the future.

5. There are sixty queens, and eighty concubines, and of young maidens there is no number. The queens are those who, out of love for the bridegroom and with an eye to the heavenly reward, beget spiritual offspring for the eternal king through the preaching of the truth and the font of holy baptism. The concubines are those who teach Christ, by preaching or baptizing, only for carnal advantage; and therefore they are designated by that perfection of the number six, through ten, because of the Decalogue. The young maidens are souls newly reborn in Christ, whose total surpasses number because of the multitude of the citizens of heaven.

6. One is my dove, my perfect one. That is, the holy and universal Church throughout the whole world. She is the only one of her mother, the chosen of her that bore her. Of her mother, that is, of the heavenly Jerusalem, which is the mother of us all. From there the grace of the Holy Spirit comes down to us, through which we are born to God. The daughters saw her and proclaimed her most blessed. Those whom he earlier called young maidens, he now names daughters; all the ancients praise the Catholic Church.

7. Who is this who comes forth like the rising dawn? The Church comes forth like the dawn, because now the rising of the true light is shown to the world after the darkness of long ignorance. Beautiful as the moon. Because, lit by the sun of justice, she illuminates the night of the world. Chosen as the sun. Because she bears the image of her maker in all justice, holiness and truth. Terrible as an army of camps set in array. Terrible to the powers of the air in the unity of charity, faith and hope.

8. I went down into the garden of nuts, to see the fruits of the valleys. For the garden of nuts is the present Church, where we hardly see one another's consciences; but when the shell of the body is broken, the fruit of inner sweetness will appear. The fruits of the valleys are the fruit of humility. The holy Church goes down through holy teachers to those who are advancing towards good fruits, or who still need the watering of teaching. And to look whether the vine had flowered, whether the pomegranates had budded. To look whether the pursuits of the virtues had flowered, and whether any were prepared, after the example of the Lord's passion, to shed their blood.

9. I did not know; my soul troubled me because of the chariots of Aminadab. I did not know the gifts of spiritual grace in you, bride; but my soul troubled me because of the bringing in of the gospel chariot, by which Aminadab (which is interpreted 'willing one of my people'), that is, Christ, is carried through the whole world. To whom the Church at once replies, consoling: Return, return, Shulamite; return, return, that we may look upon you. Do not be [given over] to yourself, but return to the knowledge of your Redeemer, who was so often promised to you in the prophets and the law. Return by purity of faith; return by perfection of works, O Shulamite, that is, captive; now from the chains of unbelief return to your Redeemer, that you may be saved.

CHAP. VII. — 1. What will you see in the Shulamite but the choirs of camps? You grieve for the hardened Synagogue: the time is near when you will see in her a choir of those fighting against the evil spirits and praising the Lord. How beautiful are your steps in sandals, daughter of the prince! Now the praises of the Church are uttered by the bridegroom himself; and first the steadfastness of works and the mortification of pleasures are praised in her, because [she is] the daughter of the prince, that is, of Christ, through the grace of baptism. [...]

2. The joints of your thighs are like necklaces, which were made by the hand of a craftsman. The concord of the two peoples, fruitful with spiritual offspring, is signified in the joint of the thighs, because just as a necklace is made by the hand of a craftsman, so [this concord] has been made firm by the ineffable generosity of our Creator. In the necklace good works are expressed.

3. Your navel is a turned bowl, never lacking drinks. The navel, that is, the frailty of our weakness, [is] a bowl when, reminded by the awareness of our mortality and weakness, we strive with ready mind to give our neighbours to drink from the cup of the saving word. Your belly is like a heap of wheat fenced about with lilies, etc. A heap of wheat is fenced about with lilies when an abundance of good work is gathered solely in the hope of everlasting light. In the belly memory is expressed; in the wheat the multiplication of good work; in the lilies chastity. Likewise in the wheat bread, and in the bowl drink, which are given to the poor, are expressed.

4. Your two breasts are like two twin fawns of a roe. Of the two breasts it was spoken above. The two breasts are the teachers of each people. In the twins are the two Testaments. Twins, on account of their single concord. Your neck is like a tower of ivory. Likewise in the neck teachers are signified, who are compared to a tower of ivory on account of their firmness and beauty, since they provide the city of God with both strength and adornment.

5. Your eyes are like the pools in Heshbon, which are in the gate of the daughter of the multitude. Likewise the eyes of the Church [are] the teachers, on account of the nourishment [they give]. And they are rightly compared to pools, because they do not cease to supply the streams of teaching to their hearers. Heshbon is interpreted 'girdle of sorrow', because the saints, instead of the vain gladness of the flesh, are bound tight with the girdle of abstinence; and well [is it said] in the gate of the multitude, because of the abundance of peoples running together through the gate of faith into the Church.

6. Your nose is like the tower of Lebanon, which looks towards Damascus. Likewise in the nose the stewards of the word of God are signified, by reason of discernment. A tower, because it holds the most eminent place in the Church; which looks towards Damascus, that is, the bloodthirsty and ungodly (for Damascus is interpreted 'drinking blood'): it signifies the carnal and cruel, against whom the holy teachers keep constant watch in the tower of Lebanon, that is, in the firmness of the Church.

7. Your head is like Carmel, and the locks of your head like the king's purple bound in channels. In the head the mind is signified, in the locks the thoughts. And just as the limbs are ruled by the head, so the thoughts are ruled by the mind. They are occupied with Carmel, that is, with lofty things, and with the passion of Christ, which is expressed by the name of purple. The channels [are] the hearts of the saints, in which such thoughts are bound.

8. How beautiful you are, and how comely, dearest, in delights. Beautiful in faith, and comely in work, dearest in delights, that is, in spiritual virtues. Your stature is likened to a palm tree. That is, the uprightness of good working always strives towards victory. And your breasts to clusters of grapes. The teachers of the Church are compared to breasts on account of the milk of first instruction, and are likened to clusters on account of the most sweet mysteries of eternity.

9. I said: I will go up into the palm tree, and take hold of its fruit, and your breasts will be like clusters of the vine. For the most victorious cross is fittingly compared to a palm tree, into which Christ ascending took hold of its fruits, that is, the gifts which he bestowed on the holy Church, which from that time has brought forth clusters of the vine, that is, holy teachers, who abound in greater knowledge and grace because of the cross and resurrection of the Saviour.

10. The scent of your mouth is like that of apples, your throat like the best wine. In the throat the voice of teaching when present is shown, in the scent the report of it when absent. And therefore the former is compared to wine on account of the fragrance of the virtues, the latter to apples on account of the sweetness of the report from afar.

11. Worthy for my beloved to drink, and for his lips and teeth to ruminate. For the bride snatched the word from the mouth of the bridegroom, when he compared her to the best wine, and added: Worthy for my beloved, that is, so great is the sublimity of the gospel preaching that the beloved himself, appearing first through it in the flesh, opened the heavenly way to the world. And for his lips and teeth, that is, he gave [it] to the apostles and the greatest preachers to meditate upon.

12. I [am] my beloved's. And no one else's; to him I devote all the care of service and love. And his turning is towards me. He loves me alone and helps me, that I may not fail on the way. Let us go out into the field, let us stay in the villages; let us rise early to the vineyards; let us see whether the vine has flowered, whether the flowers are bringing forth fruits, whether the pomegranates have flowered. For the Church is in no way able either to go forth to working well, or to stay persevering in the exercise of good working, or to rise to the path of the resolve to act well, or to discern how far the minds of her hearers have advanced, unless helped by the grace of God, who said: Behold, I am with you, etc. Likewise in the field Christians are signified, in the vineyards the churches, in the flowers faith, in the fruits the virtues, in the pomegranates martyrdom. For in each of these the bride seeks the presence of her beloved.

13. There I will give you my breasts. That is, the tutors of my little ones: for in all these the holy leaders make progress. The mandrakes have given their scent in our gardens. The mandrake, on account of its manifold kinds of remedies, is compared to the virtues of the saints: the gates of the Church are the holy teachers. In gates of this kind the mandrakes have given their scent, when each spiritual person spreads from himself the report of virtues far and wide. All fruits new and old, my beloved, I have kept for you. The fruits new and old are the precepts or promises of the New Testament and of the Old: for the Church refers all things to his grace.

CHAP. VIII. — 1. Who will grant me you as my brother, sucking the breasts of my mother, that I may find you outside? This is the ancient voice of the righteous longing for the coming of Christ in the flesh. Sucking the breasts of my mother, that is, to be born and nourished in the Synagogue according to the nature of the human condition. And that I may find you outside. The beloved was inside while in the beginning was the Word; outside, when the Word was made flesh.

2. There I may kiss you. That is, I shall see face to face, and speak mouth to mouth. And now no one may despise me. Before the coming of Christ the Church was only within the narrow bounds of Judaea; after the Ascension she was spread through the whole world, and [became] venerable. I will take hold of you. That is, I will receive you as you come with ready and faithful devotion.

3. And I will lead [you] into the house of my mother, and into the chamber of her who bore me; there you will teach me. When the dispensation of the flesh has been accomplished, I will lead you as you return, with joyful eyes, into the house of my mother. Into the house of my mother, where the heavenly Jerusalem is, our mother; there you will teach me to hope for better gifts than I had had in the law. And I will give you a cup of spiced wine. That is, fervent love, adorned with the various spices of the virtues. And the new wine of my pomegranates. That is, the triumph of the glorious holy martyrs, who with most fervent love endure the flames through which they do not hesitate to pass over to you.

4. His left hand under my head, and his right hand will embrace me. The left hand signifies the gifts of Christ's flesh, and the right hand expresses the future joys of the saints with Christ. Who is this who comes up from the desert, flowing with delights, leaning upon her beloved? The voice of the Synagogue marvelling how the Gentiles had suddenly come up from the desert into the embrace of the bridegroom. Flowing with delights, that is, with the beauty of all good things; leaning upon her beloved, referring all that she has to the grace of the beloved. Her [beloved], whom I thought was to be sent to me alone.

5. Under the apple tree I raised you up. Under the tree of the cross I called you back from everlasting death, as [I did] the apostles and the other elect from Judaea. There your mother was corrupted, there she who bore you was violated. That is, the greater part of the people, by denying Christ and choosing Barabbas, was rejected. Set me as a seal upon your heart, as a seal upon your arm. As we tie some sign on a finger to remember some thing. By the heart thought is signified, and by the arm work. If you wish to have me as bridegroom, let there be within love with unfeigned faith, and without devout work.

6. For love is strong as death, jealousy hard as hell. My love for you, O Synagogue, is strong even unto death; but your jealousy towards me was hard as hell. But turn jealousy into love, and you will be a bride to me, the bridegroom. Its lamps are lamps of fire and of flames. The lamps of love are the hearts of the faithful; of fire, on account of the fervour of the heart; of flames, on account of the effectiveness of working.

7. Many waters will not be able to quench love, nor will rivers overwhelm it. By many waters and rivers he means the assaults of temptations, which visibly or invisibly do not cease to attack the souls of the faithful, [but] to which love does not yield. If a man gives all the substance of his house for love, he will despise it as nothing. The saints truly despised the substance of their whole house as nothing for the greatness of their love.

8. Our sister is little, and she has no breasts. This signifies the first times of the Church being born from the Gentiles, when she was still both small in number and less fit to preach the word of God, as though the bridegroom had said of her to the Synagogue: What shall we do for our sister on the day when she is to be spoken to? As if he were saying openly: The Church of the Gentiles is indeed small in number, and is not yet able to undertake the ministry of the word. What then seems to you, O Synagogue, should be done about our sister when she is to be spoken to, that is, led to faith through the ministry of the word? The Synagogue keeping silent, the bridegroom himself answers what ought to be done.

9. If she is a wall, let us build upon it bulwarks of silver. As if he were saying: If she has in her some who are strong in faith, distinguished in intellect, or trained in philosophy, let us add to them bulwarks of silver, that is, the knowledge of the divine Scriptures, so that by it they may more easily protect the weak and the unlearned. If she is a door, let us join it together with boards of cedar. If they are simple, yet eager with zeal for teaching, let us set before them the examples of the righteous of former times, so that they may fulfil the work of teaching more surely and more effectively. The cedars signify the virtues of the saints, and the boards the breadth of love. To these very things the Church answers.

10. I am a wall, and my breasts are like a tower. From the time I became in his sight as one finding peace, I have been built together of living stones, and joined by the glue of love, and built upon an immovable foundation. The breasts, that is, the teachers, are very strong, like a tower, who know both how to nourish the little ones and how to drive out all [the attacks] of the wicked one; and this has befallen me from the time when Christ reconciled me, and through him I found peace.

11. My peaceable one had a vineyard in that which holds peoples. The vineyard, that is, the catholic Church abounding in the fruit of faith, belonged to the peaceable one, that is, to Christ, because he made peace for all things in heaven and on earth, in that congregation which possesses many peoples from the whole world, not Judaea alone. It is handed over to keepers: the prophets, or the apostles, or the angelic powers and dignities.

12. But a man for the fruit, that is, for the eternal reward of this vineyard, brings a thousand pieces of silver. That is, for the gaining of the heavenly kingdom, which is the fruit of the vineyard, he has left all things that are of the world. The number one thousand is put for perfection. That is, one who has left all things. The pieces of silver are to be taken for all money. My vineyard is before me. The voice of the bridegroom. Nevertheless, even though I entrust you to other keepers, yet I always hold you in my presence, seeing and rewarding the devotion of your labour in all things. The thousand are yours, O peaceable one. Your thousand, understood: pieces of silver. As though he had said: He who for love of me gives up all that is his will be in peace, because he gives up all his substance, which is signified by the thousand, for the love of God.

13. And two hundred to those who keep its fruits. These are the holy teachers, who give up all things of the world and do not cease to labour in the word of preaching; these are given a double reward with me, which is signified by the two hundred. You who dwell in the gardens, friends are listening. Since our conversation must be ended, having heard this last farewell from me: dwell always in the gardens of the virtues; and know that friends, that is, the angelic spirits and the souls of the saints, always regard you and rejoice at the sight of you. Make me hear your voice. That is, let the voice of your preaching always be heard by me, while you are able.

14. Flee, my beloved. As if she were saying openly: Since, appearing in the flesh, you deigned to bestow on me the precepts and gifts of heavenly life, now that these are accomplished, return into the bosom of the Father, O beloved. Be like a roe, and a young hart, upon the mountains of spices. And let this be my comfort: since I cannot behold you with continual sight, at least remember to console me with frequent visitation.
